title: Rainy Day in Seoul? 10 Indoor Places to Go (Plus What Locals Do When It Rains)
html:
Rain on your Seoul trip? Don't worry — it doesn't have to ruin your day. Seoul is full of big indoor spaces: huge museums (many of them free), an indoor theme park, a giant library inside a shopping mall, K-pop experience centers, and cozy neighborhoods full of cafés and pubs. Most of them sit right next to a subway station, so you can spend the whole day hopping between them and barely get wet.

Below are 10 rainy-day ideas, grouped by what kind of traveler you are. You don't need to see them all — pick two or three that are close to each other (the table near the end helps with that) and enjoy a slower day.

Before You Go: Rainy-Day Basics in Seoul

A few simple things make a rainy day in Seoul much easier:

  • Forgot your umbrella? Every convenience store (CU, GS25, 7-Eleven — they're on almost every corner) sells umbrellas, usually for around ₩5,000–10,000. Many subway station shops sell them too, as soon as it starts to rain.
  • Use the subway, not the bus. The subway runs underground, so rain doesn't slow it down. Buses and taxis get stuck in traffic when it rains, and taxis become hard to find.
  • Stay underground. Big stations like Jamsil, Samseong (COEX), and Gangnam connect straight into shopping malls and underground shopping streets. You can often walk from the train to the building without going outside.
  • Check the weather in the morning. Summer (especially July) brings Korea's rainy season, called jangma, with heavy downpours. On those days, plan for indoor places only.

What locals actually do on a rainy day: many Koreans head to a small restaurant for pajeon (a crispy savory pancake with green onions) and makgeolli (a milky, lightly sweet rice wine). People say the sizzling sound of the pancake in the pan sounds like rain, so the two just go together. If you see a sign that says 전 (jeon) on a rainy evening, you've found the right place — try it!

A rainy night on Yanghwa-ro, near Hongdae. Photo: Tony, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

1. Lotte World Adventure & Seoul Sky (Jamsil)

Lotte World Adventure is one of the biggest indoor theme parks in the world. Most of the rides, parades, and shows are under a giant glass roof, so rain doesn't matter much. (There's also an outdoor section called Magic Island on the lake, but some of its rides may close in heavy rain.) A one-day ticket at the gate costs about ₩62,000 for adults, but foreign visitors can usually get a big discount by booking online in advance through sites like Klook or Trazy — bring your passport to show you're a foreigner.

Right next door is Lotte World Tower, the tallest building in Korea. Its observation deck, Seoul Sky, is on the 117th–123rd floors and costs around ₩31,000–33,000 for adults. One honest tip: on a very cloudy day you may see only white fog from the top. If the clouds are low, do the theme park first and check the view later — sometimes the sky clears in the evening. Both are connected to Jamsil Station (Line 2 & Line 8), and you can walk from the station into the buildings without going outside.

Lotte World Tower (home of Seoul Sky) behind Lotte World's Magic Island and Seokchon Lake. Photo: kallerna, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

2. National Museum of Korea (Yongsan)

If you only visit one museum in Seoul, make it this one. The National Museum of Korea is huge — you could spend a whole rainy day inside — and the permanent exhibition is free. It covers Korean history from the Stone Age to the last Korean kingdom, with gold crowns, pottery, Buddhist art, and more. There are English signs everywhere, plus cafés and a food court inside, so you don't need to go out for lunch.

It's open every day (except New Year's Day and the two biggest Korean holidays, Seollal and Chuseok), and stays open until 9pm on Wednesdays and Saturdays. Take the subway to Ichon Station (Line 4, Exit 2) — an underground walkway takes you most of the way. Note: from July 2026 until late January 2027, a few galleries (Buddhist art, metal crafts, and some painting rooms) are closed for renovation, but most of the museum is open.

The National Museum of Korea in Yongsan. Photo: Ethan Doyle White, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

3. War Memorial of Korea (Yongsan)

The War Memorial of Korea tells the story of the Korean War (1950–1953) and why Korea is still divided into North and South today. Even if you're not into military history, it helps you understand modern Korea much better. Inside you'll find large, well-made exhibits with English explanations, and a hall honoring soldiers from the many countries that fought with the UN. Admission is free, and it's closed on Mondays.

It's just two subway stops from the National Museum of Korea, so the two make an easy pair for one rainy day. Get off at Samgakji Station (Line 4 or Line 6) and walk a few minutes. Outside there's a big collection of real tanks and planes — skip that part if it's pouring and focus on the indoor halls.

The main building of the War Memorial of Korea. Photo: Adbar, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

4. National Palace Museum of Korea (Gyeongbokgung)

Planned to visit Gyeongbokgung, Seoul's biggest royal palace, but the rain ruined it? Walking around the palace's open courtyards in heavy rain isn't much fun — but the National Palace Museum sits right inside the palace grounds and is a great backup. It shows the real treasures of Korea's last royal family, the Joseon dynasty (1392–1910): royal robes, thrones, seals, and even a royal car used by the last kings.

Admission is free, and you don't need a palace ticket to enter the museum. It's a short walk from Gyeongbokgung Station (Line 3, Exit 5). It closes on a few days a year (including major holidays), so check the official website before you go. If the rain stops, the palace is right there waiting for you.

The National Palace Museum of Korea, inside the Gyeongbokgung Palace grounds. Photo: Mobius6, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

5. COEX: Starfield Library & SEA LIFE Aquarium (Gangnam)

COEX is one of Asia's largest underground shopping malls, which makes it perfect for a rainy day. In the middle is the famous Starfield Library — a two-story space with 13-meter-tall bookshelves that you've probably seen on Instagram. It's free to enter, open roughly 10:30am–10pm, and you can sit and read or just take photos.

In the same mall is the SEA LIFE COEX Aquarium, with sharks, manatees, penguins, and a long underwater tunnel. Walk-up tickets are around ₩35,000 for adults, but booking online in advance is usually about 20% cheaper. Around both, you'll find hundreds of shops, a big food court, and a movie theater. Take the subway to Samseong Station (Line 2) or Bongeunsa Station (Line 9) — both connect straight into the mall.

The giant bookshelves of Starfield Library in COEX Mall. Photo: Sgroey, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

6. HiKR Ground (K-pop & K-drama Experience)

For K-pop and K-drama fans, HiKR Ground is a must — and it's completely free. Run by the Korea Tourism Organization, this five-floor building lets you step inside Korean pop culture: stand on music-video-style sets, try dance games, record in a mini studio, and take photos in scenes that look like they're from a drama. There's a café on the top floor.

It's open Tuesday to Sunday (closed Mondays). The 1st and 5th floors are open 10am–9pm, and floors 2–4 close at 7pm, so go earlier in the day to see everything. Most people spend 1–2 hours. It's by the Cheonggyecheon stream downtown, about a 5-minute walk from Jonggak Station (Line 1) or Euljiro 1-ga Station (Line 2).

Inside HiKR Ground. Photo: Zero guk, CC BY-SA 2.0 KR, via Wikimedia Commons.

7. K-Culture VR Tower (N Seoul Tower)

N Seoul Tower sits on top of Namsan Mountain in the middle of the city. On a rainy day the view from the top is usually just clouds — but inside the tower building there's a fun indoor option: the K-Culture VR Tower, a small theater dedicated to K-pop in virtual reality. You put on a VR headset and watch idol concert performances and music videos as if you were standing right in front of the stage.

Shows start every hour from about 10am to 9pm and last around 20–40 minutes. Tickets are sold on booking sites like Trazy and on-site; check the current price before you go. It's not recommended for children under 13. To get up the mountain without a long wet walk, take the Namsan shuttle bus (numbers 01A or 01B) from downtown, or the Namsan cable car.

N Seoul Tower on Namsan, home of the K-Culture VR Tower. Photo: lumoplank, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

8. Seoul Botanic Park (Magok)

Want some green even on a gray day? Seoul Botanic Park has a huge glass greenhouse full of tropical and Mediterranean plants from 12 cities around the world — banana trees, giant cacti, olive trees, and more. Inside it's warm and bright, and listening to rain on the glass roof is actually pretty relaxing.

Greenhouse entry is just ₩5,000 for adults. It's open 9:30am–6pm (March–October) and 9:30am–5pm (November–February), and closed on Mondays. Take the subway to Magongnaru Station (Line 9 or the Airport Railroad, AREX). Because it's on the airport line, it's a nice stop on your last day before flying out of Gimpo or Incheon.

The glass greenhouse at Seoul Botanic Park. Photo: Korea.net / Korean Culture and Information Service, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

9. Insadong (Tea Houses & Craft Shops)

Insadong is an old neighborhood full of traditional craft shops, art galleries, and small tea houses. It's partly outdoors, so bring an umbrella — but on a light-rain day it's lovely, and there are lots of places to duck inside. The main street is lined with shops selling hanji (traditional Korean paper), ceramics, calligraphy brushes, and souvenirs.

Don't miss Ssamziegil, a shopping building with a gentle spiral walkway that climbs past small craft stores. Then sit down in a traditional tea house for a warm cup of yuja-cha (citron tea) or daechu-cha (jujube tea) while you watch the rain. Get off at Anguk Station (Line 3, Exit 6) and walk a couple of minutes.

Insadong-gil, the main street of Insadong. Photo: Epicgenius, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

10. Hongdae & Itaewon: Pubs, Live Music, and K-pop Bars

When the rain keeps going into the evening, head to Hongdae (the lively area around Hongik University) or Itaewon (Seoul's most international neighborhood). Both are packed with restaurants, pubs, live music bars, and clubs, so you can hop from one to the next with only a short walk in between.

A fun idea for K-pop fans: spend the night hopping between bars, restaurants, and cafés that play K-pop music videos all day. In Hongdae especially, there are K-pop themed pocha — a pocha is a casual Korean pub where you eat bar snacks with soju or beer — where the big screens show idol videos non-stop and everyone sings along. It's also the perfect time to try that rainy-day combo of pajeon and makgeolli. For Hongdae, take the subway to Hongik University Station (Line 2 / AREX); for Itaewon, go to Itaewon Station (Line 6).

A Hongdae street at night. Photo: Sgroey, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Quick Pick: Which Rainy-Day Spot Is Right for You?

Place Nearest station Cost (adult) Time needed Best for

Seoul Botanic ParkMagongnaru (Line 9/AREX)₩5,000 (closed Mon)1.5–2 hoursNature lovers, last day

Easy combos for one rainy day: National Museum of Korea + War Memorial (both in Yongsan, two subway stops apart) · National Palace Museum + Insadong tea house (15 minutes apart) · COEX in the afternoon + Lotte World Tower at night (both on Line 2) · HiKR Ground by day + Hongdae K-pop bars at night. One more idea: the non-verbal comedy show NANTA in Myeongdong, where chefs make music with kitchen tools, is fun for all ages and needs no Korean at all.

☔ Got rain in the forecast for your Seoul dates? Tell us in the comments what you're into, and we'll help you pick the best indoor plan!
meta_description: Rain in Seoul? 10 indoor spots for a wet day: free museums, Lotte World, Starfield Library, HiKR Ground K-pop, botanic greenhouse, and cozy Hongdae pubs.
